items.article: The mint flavor of San Francisco's favorite It's-It ice cream cookie sandwiches has changed color. A major change has come for San Francisco’s beloved It’s-It ice cream sandwiches. The mint flavor of the ice cream cookie sandwich , once an ostentatiously loud shade of green, has changed color, as first spotted by the San Francisco Chronicle. (The Chronicle and SFGATE are both owned by Hearst but have separate newsrooms.) An SFGATE editor bought a box at Andronico’s and confirmed the breaking news — the bright, toothpaste-green ice cream had been drained of color, with a far more muted, pale pastel green in its place. Where the shade once screamed “GREEN!” at the top of its lungs, now, it only whispered. Curiously, though, It’s-It has mostly kept the change quiet. Despite SFGATE’s repeated attempts this week to reach the Burlingame-based company for comment, It’s-It never got back to us. The company has not released any statement announcing the change to its customers, and photos of the mint ice cream sandwich on its website remain the same , advertising the old seafoam green color instead of the new, lighter shade. It’s-It President Charles Shamieh did speak with the Chronicle, telling the outlet that It’s-It made the change due to U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Washington DC is known for its monuments, museums and political history. But the nation's capital also has plenty of ghost stories and haunted legends. From the White House to the U.S. Capitol, some of the city's most famous buildings are said to have ghostly visitors. Georgetown, one of Washington's oldest neighborhoods, has its own collection of spooky stories, while the Octagon House is often considered one of the city's most haunted places. Ford's Theatre, forever linked to the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln, has also become part of DC's haunted lore. Whether you believe in ghosts or not, these stories offer a different way to look at some of the capital's most familiar places.
